text: Every KQL query in Chapter 2 ended with a table of rows and columns. The render operator is simply the next pipe stage after that table, telling the query engine, or a workbook's query step, how to draw it instead of listing it. Nothing about the rows changes -- render doesn't filter, aggregate, or transform data the way where or summarize do.

Take SigninLogs, filtered to the last 24 hours, summarized into FailedCount by bin of TimeGenerated over 1 hour, then render timechart. That's a display instruction appended at the very end, after the real work of shaping the data is already done -- which is why the columns a query produces before render matter more than the render line itself.

Three render types cover most Sentinel needs, and each expects a different column shape. Timechart wants a time column plus a numeric column, plotted over time -- built for how something changed. Piechart wants a category plus a number, shown as proportions, and stops being readable past six or seven slices. Barchart handles that same category-plus-number shape but reads better with more categories.

Timechart fits the failed-login example exactly, because bin(TimeGenerated) gives it a time axis to plot against. Piechart fits something like sign-ins by result type or alerts by severity, where share of the whole is the useful framing. Barchart fits the same shape as piechart, but wins once exact comparison between bars matters more than proportion.

Running render timechart directly in the Logs blade shows that chart immediately -- useful for exploring a query before ever opening a workbook. Inside a workbook's query step, though, the chart type is usually set through the step's own visualization settings dropdown, because the workbook editor offers additional layout and formatting controls render alone doesn't expose.

Either path reads the same underlying signal: shape the query's output columns correctly, and both the raw render line and the workbook's chart-type picker know what to do with them. Next up, Lesson 16 puts all of this together -- building a full workbook for one specific, real use case.
